utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Welcome back to the courtroom as we approach the last lap of the evidence. Before we resume the evidence, there are a couple of matters I ought to deal with administratively. The first of these is to ensure that I have the order of witnesses this week correct. We anticipate hearing from Professor Zivojin Aleksic, Dr. Zoran Stankovic, Professor Radomir Lukic, and General Milan Djakovic, who is to be called as a Chamber witness. I see no one rising to correct me on the order, so I assume that that is accurate. The Chamber has been trying for some time to sort out the issue of which edition of the VJ rules of service applied at the relevant time. It appears to be agreed now that the edition of 1996 is the relevant edition. However, the Chamber does not have a full copy of the 1996 edition. Does anyone possess that item?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, what we've done to save having CLSS translate the entire 1996 edition is simply check to see if there's anything in the 1996 edition that differs from the 1994 edition in any relevant area, and we spent quite a lot of time going through that process and discovered that there is only one section, and I sent that off to Grant Dawson an hour or so ago explaining that there is this one section that we've sent off to CLSS which should be finished with translation today. And we'll offer that as a separate exhibit; otherwise, 1994 is either irrelevant or authoritative because there is no change in the language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think there remains the problem, Mr. Ackerman, that 1994 has been referred to from time to time in a context in which it may be identical to 1996, and it's being sure that the evidence accurately reflects the terms -- or at least the judgement accurately reflect the terms of the 1996 edition.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We were aware of that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That concerns us. And what would be -- are you saying you have a full copy of the 1996 version?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, but it's a fairly large book, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm not suggesting it needs to be translated, but the Chamber would like to have that document to see which parts of it ought to be translated, if any, beyond those that you've already made arrangements for.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can make arrangements to deliver it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, could you do that in the first instance informally?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And secondly, we would require the parties, and I don't think this is controversial, to stipulate that the 1996 version is the accurate one. And we may require a stipulation in due course about the extent to which 1996 and 1994 are identical, but that would require our review of the situation. But if you will in the first instance give us the 1996 version informally, we will then issue an order that deals with the resolution of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I've been in touch with Mr. Hannis about this, and we basically agree, and if you want a stipulation on the record, I think we can do that now rather than something in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no reason to doubt that the 1996 version is the applicable authoritative one. I'm willing to do that. I haven't seen it myself to see how the numbers differ, but if Mr. Ackerman's going to deliver that to the Court and you're going to look at it, I have no reason not to stipulate to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's make that stage one, Mr. Ackerman. If you would deliver that to Mr. Dawson, we will then issue an order. It may be an oral order tomorrow in the course of this week that clarifies the position about what's expected of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll see that it is delivered by tomorrow, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And that leaves so far as administrative issues are concerned anything that needs to be said before Professor Aleksic gives evidence. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just one thing, Your Honour, I had indicated that I might be requesting that my cross-examination be postponed until tomorrow because I was awaiting some information. It came earlier than I expected, so I'm ready to go forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's very helpful. I can indicate that the Chamber was sympathetic to your request, and that's why arrangements were made to try to advance the evidence of Dr. Stankovic in case there was a gap, but you reassure us, so we can now proceed. Mr. Visnjic, your witness, is he ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my witness is here, and he's in the witness room. Before the witness comes in, I would just like to say a few words with regard to procedural matters. Mr. Ackerman said that they would be calling their own handwriting expert, but he didn't say anything about it now. Could he please state whether they will be calling such a witness or not so that we can organize Professor Aleksic's stay here, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We're not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Our next witness is Professor Zivojin Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Fine. Thank you. I have some problem with the right leg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're comfortable sitting, though, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which language are you going to use?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] I prefer Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, feel free to choose yourself which language you wish to address us in, but you may feel most comfortable with your first language, and we understand that. You'll now be examined by Mr. Visnjic on behalf of Mr. Ojdanic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, good afternoon yet again.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Professor, on the 26th of February, 1998, you gave your own opinion with regard to certain questions put to you by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: That is 3D -- I'm sorry. I meant 2008, the 26th of February, 2008. During the proofing, you looked at these findings?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Then on the 11th of May, you submitted some additional information to the Defence in relation to your own findings?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: They have been admitted as 3D 1148, whereas your basic findings are 3D 1140. Professor, you also provided some basic information in respect of your CV. That is 3D 1141. And then you submitted additional information by way of Exhibit 3D 1146. Have you had a look at this?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I meant these documents. Also, you submitted to the Defence a decision of the Ministry of Justice appointing you a court expert. That is 3D 1147. Professor, do you have any objections in relation to these documents that you had during the proofing for this testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: No, except that there has been this rejuvenation; that is, at the age of 77 I've been asked to prove that I'm a court expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to show you some exhibits, and you're going to tell me whether those are the documents that you used when working on your expert opinion. I would like the witness to be shown 3D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before we lose track of this, Mr. Visnjic, let us be clear. Professor, the original report, which was 3D 1140, is that an accurate account of the findings you made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, we were given a document which I think is 3D 1148 called a supplemental information sheet. Have you seen that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so, or did we? I really don't know by way of these numbers. What is this all about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, indeed I got the impression that we were going through a ritual rather than looking at the terms of your investigation. Would you have a look, please, at 3D 1148.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Please. [Interpretation] What was that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, does that also accurately record your findings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. When working on the first document, I provided my basic findings, but now since I had time before arriving here, I used some modern optical equipment, and I established certain things, so I thought it might be right to present to the Court these findings of mine, as well, if it would assist the Court in its deliberations and decision-making.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Professor, now I'm going to show you a few exhibits, and could you please confirm to us whether these are the exhibits that you used while working on your expert opinion and findings. So could I please have 3D 1108 called up.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I don't see anything over here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It will appear in a moment or so on your screen --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, yes, yes. This is one of the documents that I looked at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Our electronic court exhibit system is not quite as sharp as some brains.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, thank you, but I've slowed down myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 3D 1130.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have had a look at that document too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Professor, can you explain to us the procedure involved. How did it come about that you had a look at the document that is before you now?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, as you know, you made a request to me with regard to four questions, I believe, and since you obtained a permit, I accompanied you to the military archives or part of the military archives where I was shown some originals. And while you were talking to them, I stayed there for about three or four hours and had a look at the originals. Actually, in my profession, one pays attention to the originals, especially the back page of the original to see whether it had been scanned. When I was assured that what I was looking at was not a scan, I asked for photocopies to be made of the document that I saw, and after less than two months I got the original, too, and then I worked on my expert opinion. Before that, I had a look at the originals, but then I got these excellent photocopies, in colour, at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let's just clarify this because in line 23 in the transcript it says something. What did you get in colour, the photocopies or the original?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Photocopies, photocopies. You know what it's like when you're in archives. I looked at archives that are not open to the public. I had a look at the original there under some very vigilant eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I'd like you to have a look at 3D 1109.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had a look at that log-book, too, in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And right after that, 3D 1131, please. Professor, can you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the log. This is the cover page of the log that I examined in the original, like the rest, and then I received photocopies.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And finally could the witness please be shown P1459.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have had a look at this and another document of the same content.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D 1106.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. It's actually two documents of identical contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you also said to us that you received colour photocopies of these documents?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, these are documents 3D 1132 and 3D 1133.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The photocopies are 3D 1132 and 33; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are colour photocopies, colour copies of the exhibits; or more specifically, 3D 1132 is a colour photocopy of 3D 1106, and 3D 1133 is a colour copy of Exhibit P1459.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The ones with the earlier numbers P1459 and 3D 1106, what are they? Are they scanned copies or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, these are black and white copies, out of which one was a Prosecution exhibit, and the other one was a Defence exhibit, General Ojdanic's Defence exhibit. Both were obtained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just to show us the difference, would you put 3D 1132 on the screen, please. Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we also wish to submit or to have admitted into evidence a conclusion of the Government of Serbia along with a decision of the national committee on submitting documentation, and the number would be 3D 1134. So I would just like to have that recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm confused about this last document, 3D 1134. If it could be put on the screen, maybe I'll know what it is, but it doesn't sound like something that has anything to do with this expertise, but I don't know until I see it. I just don't know what it is, but I don't think you can get a document admitted just by saying, Here's the document number, please admit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Apparently this document is already admitted, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, I know what it is now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're content with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Professor, your expert report contains sufficient information. I will not ask you in detail about these issues, but could you provide additional information, please, about the supplemental information. So could we see 3D 1148, please, the last page of that document, which is a table that you prepared.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. This has to do with a numerator; is that what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I think -- I see that here we see the black-and-white version. We will try to find you the colour one.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, the colour is crucial here, and I used a microscope, a stereo microscope with a light that comes at an angle, so that is quite important. Could we please see the colour picture -- well, actually, wait, I have a copy if that is of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, perhaps we could put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there an exhibit that's coloured with a different number?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I was surprised when I saw the black-and-white version. I thought that we would see a colour version on our screens because that's what we have provided, distributed, to everyone. When we forwarded it electronically, we sent the colour copy to everyone, and I see that on the screen we have the black-and-white copy. We'll probably have to replace it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, on the left side. [Interpretation] I produced a number of these copies, so if you can't find them I can leave you my copies or at least this copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, do you have a spare colour copy I could have, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have it too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's just I was surprised that the one in front of me from the ELMO is described as in colour, whereas the one that I'm shown is much more colourful, and you don't need to substitute anything. Once we see this on the ELMO, we can give it an IC number as long as we are sure we're using the right one. So please continue, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Professor, could you explain briefly what did you find in comparing these copies?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. If you look at the colour copy, I don't think it is necessary to speak to the Chamber about the numerator. That's the equipment that puts stamps on documents, and if you want to use it additionally, then you use a needle to move the number. Sometimes you use the same numerator, sometimes a different one. If you look at the first two, you see that there is a change in calibre, very visible one, in relation to the others, and figure 2 is especially prominent. Figure 6, partially prominent, but if you look at 2 and 6 in the third semble, you will see that they are much narrower and slimmer. What is the case here? People who use numerators also occasionally antedate something. When they use a needle to change the date or the month or the year - in this particular case number 2 is the most prominent one - then this moving with the needle takes figure 2 back into its original location, but it's very hard to put it in its exact original location, to pin-point it. In my practice, I have never come across a situation where when one moves the numerator, figure 2 goes back to its original position. Your Honours, I would like to point out that between these two first samples, figure 2 did not go back to its original position. So even between the first two samples, you could see that there is a difference or a discrepancy there. Unfortunately, when you're dealing with secret documents from archives, then you can't really insist on going into even deeper analysis. However, I think, with all due respect to the Chamber, I would like to draw your attention to the fact that this figure 2 in the date 26 is really prominent; it sticks out. I selected figure 2 because you can see an optical -- rather, figure 26 because there's an optical difference, and, also, there's a difference in colour. Initially I thought that these dots -- or rather, full stops after figure 6 and figure 5 could indicate that these full stops or dots are not completely identical. You have to bear in mind that these figures can also be affected by the ink-pad containing more colour but can also be affected by the surface that they land on. However, in this particular case we have a different situation. The colour is completely different in the first two samples, then figure 2 is of a prominently different calibre, and when you compare that to how it's written and if you compare it to this line that goes on top of the figures that I drew, then you can see how slanted this is, this line going from 2 to 99, which leads me to conclude, Your Honours, and it's not always easy to do it when analysing handwriting, but it leads me to conclude that these two dates were antedated and that they were done after the following six samples. If you need additional explanation, I'm available to provide it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it you meant -- well, could you repeat the last part of your answer. It led you to conclude that these two dates were ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you speak up, please? The volume is not right. I'm addressing the interpreter now. Could you please speak up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The translation into English doesn't make sense. The first part is contradicted by the second part. Could you explain again what conclusion you reached about these first two.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The conclusion that I came to concerns 26.05.1999, the first two samples, the ones in the colour version. They differ both in terms of calibre and the ink colour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you then you said something about the time at which they were applied to the page. Could you tell us again your conclusion on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very hard to say, but one thing is certain. The stamp was not placed at the time when the date was set in the numerator; rather, it was done afterwards, after some time had passed. Perhaps if we're provided a spectrum analysis, we could establish more, but it wasn't possible to establish more based on a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't have additional questions for the witness. All the questions I wanted to put and answers to them can be found in Professor's report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you clarify one thing for me. Is this table on the screen part of the supplementary information sheet?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's part of the supplemental information sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can we give an IC number to the exhibit that's been used?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, page 3 of 3D 1148 in colour would be IC196.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Professor Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to begin talking a little bit about your CV and the things that are contained in there. As near as I can tell by reading it, you spent most of your career as a professor of law at the University of Belgrade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, but in 1963 I received a master of art level type by -- from Professor Bishof in Lausanne who is one of the greatest experts in the field of criminology and also handwriting. So I received this title from three schools in Lausanne: Medical school, law school, and that of political sciences. And then I received a Ph.D. title. If it can be of assistance, I published 28 books, out of which at least three or four were devoted to handwriting and document analysis. I hope the Chamber will understand that I, while I taught at the law school, did not also want to work as a court expert, although it's been more than 50 years since I received that title. However, I made myself available to the state authorities, and in that time I was involved in almost all trials against Ustashas and terrorists attacking our diplomatic staff and I provided various reports to the state authorities --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're going way, way beyond what I asked you. The only question I asked you was, are you a professor of law? Now, you can just say yes. You don't have to give me the story of your life. I'm not asking for that, okay?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: What do you mean? We are discussing my life here, and I'm quite grateful to -- for all the questions put to me because you're giving me an opportunity to praise myself starting from 1977. Not only am I a professor, but all of these lawyers here were my students, and they can confirm that to you, and I am quite proud of them because all of them are better than I am. Please go ahead. I'm really proud of them, and they are much better than I ever was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I feel sort of deficient and abused that I didn't get to be one of your students.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: It hasn't been translated to me what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to ask you some more questions --

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Ackerman, you have such a reputation that you ought not to have been able to acquire had you been my student.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's an answer for analysis.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Ackerman come closer to the microphone. The interpreters can barely hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You became a court expert only after you retired from Belgrade University as a law professor, true?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I did not want to fail as an expert and thus disappoint my law students.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, it says that you have lectured on criminalistics in America. Where did you lecture on criminalistics in America?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I taught in many places, from Japan through Asia and Africa to America.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, no, no. I just want to know where in America did you lecture on criminalistics? Just answer the question I ask you, please.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, you are now attacking my memory. You are attributing great importance to the United States. I respect that. But let me tell you, I worked for the United Nations as an expert for narcotics back in 1968 or 1969. Then I attended several congresses where I gave lectures, and I lectured with the late Milton Helpern in New York, who is a chief medical lector, and I also taught at Berkeley's, and I could probably if I tried hard enough remember where I taught in other countries. At any rate, while I was an active professor --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you teach handwriting analysis in America? Did you lecture on handwriting analysis in America?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: On that topic as well. There was a congress devoted to that topic with people from Canada and the United States attending, but with Their Honours' leave I would say just this before the cross-examination process. I was given a task to provide an expert report. I provided expert report, and I think that it is a better testament than everything I have done in my career, everywhere I went, travelled, and taught. I received a number of awards in Germany, from various other associations. I taught, as I said, at the invitation of Milton Helpern, who died, and you're probably familiar with Joe Hazard who taught at the Columbia University. He and I were co-chairmen of the World Association of Law Professors. I taught at his school, as well, I lectured on different topics. I couldn't really remember all of the topics right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, you're plainly a multi-talented individual, but the concern of this Trial Chamber is in relation to the matter of handwriting analysis, and the questions you're being asked are quite rightly confined to your expertise in that field. And it's perfectly legitimate for counsel to explore the extent to which you are recognised as an expert in this field, and Mr. Ackerman is, therefore, asking you the extent to which you have lectured in the United States on the subject of handwriting and document analysis. Could you deal with that specifically because it would be of great help to us also.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, first of all, let me start from the beginning. I'll start from the beginning. Why would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- Professor, please don't start from the beginning. Please answer Mr. Ackerman's question. Where have you lectured in the United States on the subject of handwriting and document analysis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't give you an accurate answer to that question. As a visiting professor in Japan, I went there to teach one topic, and I ended up teaching six others. I simply can't remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, if you haven't done so, please just say so, and if you can't remember, please say so. But that would be rather strange, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I taught with Milton Helpern in New York and also with Larry Alanbear who was a chief on drug addiction. I taught there about forgeries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. So these were lectures about handwriting and document analysis, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Forgeries of prescriptions, medical prescriptions, to obtain narcotics. What I wanted to show you is the diploma awarded to me by Mr. Bishof, who is the top expert for handwriting. He issued this diploma to me. His institute was in existence for 50 years, and at that point only nine of us had graduated from that institute. But forgive me, I am old, and perhaps I go into too much detail. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Ackerman, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Milton Helpern was an pathologist in the medical examiner for the city of New York, wasn't he? He didn't have anything to do with handwriting, did he?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you said in the --

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Larry Alanbear did have to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You said in the CV that in the 11 years you've been doing this work, you have written 1.200 expert reports. Now, that works out to about eight or nine a month or about two a week. Do you write two expert reports a week?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I don't think that you can count it that way, but let's see. Starting from 1976 -- or rather, from 19 -- I retired in 1996, so let's say starting from 1997, it's been 11 years. I have over 1.000 expert reports, some done independently by me, some done within a team. However, starting in 1974, when I graduated from this institute in Lausanne in Switzerland, I was invited to provide expert opinion in various cases whenever needed, including handwriting issues --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm asking you about what you say in your CV, and what you say in your CV in paragraph 4 of the supplement is that since you became a permanent court expert on documents and handwriting for that 11 years, you have written 1.200 expert reports. Now, did you just tell us that's not true and some of those were written by some team and that you really haven't written 1.200 reports? Because if you have, you have written two a week. Have you done that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, looking at the figures, yes, but the work is not evenly distributed. Some weeks there's more work; some weeks there's less work. I also included in this figure private expert report work that I did in Belgrade. In Belgrade, the court can ask an expert to provide a report, and occasionally parties in a case very frequently want handwriting on last wills to be analysed by an expert. So let's say that I was a fashionable expert for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. You want to stand by this 1.200 that you've written in 11 years?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. You say in paragraph 1 of your supplement that you've published two books relating to the subject of graphoscopy. Tell me, the first of those, what's the name of it; where was it published; what year was it published?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: The first title was "Expert Analysis Of Handwriting And Documents," and it was published by let's say Partenon or Glossarium publishers. The second such document was published --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... published where?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, in Belgrade. Partenon or Glossarium, one of these two publishers, because the other books on that topic were published by Partenon -- no, Glossarium, then this must have been done by Partenon. Your Honours, that is a specialised title of the book, and later on --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was written by you, was it? Did you write it? Did you write all the words in it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, we use various sources. When you write about Roman law, you use sources including what famous experts on the topic said. Now, in your question I suppose there's more curiosity than anything else, any other motive, and naturally I condensed or used the latest findings that kept changing over time. The second book, since one of the greatest handwriting experts from Zagreb came to Belgrade and got his Ph.D. title with me - his name was Sabor - he was an inspiration for me, and then I produced the new book. There are two books in total with that title. Perhaps the second one is somewhat expanded because I saw that expert analysis of handwriting is done more often in civil cases and before commercial courts than in criminal cases. So this other book was called "Establishing The Truth By Way Of Analysing Handwriting In Civil Cases And Criminal Cases." So these are the two books, so one publisher was called Partenon, and the other publisher was called Glossarium.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What year was the first one published?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll tell you, but I have to try to remember. When I published the first ten of my books, the ones I wrote completely on my own, then this manuscript was published as the third book --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... graphoscopy, when was that first took that you told us about published? When? Just tell us what year. If you don't remember, say so.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: One was published just before I retired, and the other one was published once I retired, if that's what you're really interested in. I do reserve the right to give a more extensive response to this, but I don't want to upset you or the Judge. But when one writes in the field of criminalistics, and my book on criminalistics had 15 editions, a considerable portion was devoted to handwriting analysis. Then in a separate writing, I wrote about that too. This -- these books were written up until 1996, and the others afterwards. If I -- or rather, 1992, if I remember correctly now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If someone says that what you did is simply translate books written by other people in the field and publish them, would they be wrong about that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, you know what, there is vanity among opera pre-Madonnas, and there is vanity among scholars too. I'm sorry that you came across such a person. You could have come across quite a few other people. There's other people like this, too, but I really cannot protest against a phantom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, is -- what's the answer to my question? Would that person be wrong if that's what they said about you?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, you are challenging or questioning my integrity, but I am going to reply because I respect this Court. I was not somebody who copied other people's work. I never did any such thing, and that's for a simple reason. People believe that I am the founder of criminalistics in Yugoslavia and that I introduced that subject at the law school of our university. That would be my basic answer. If you have something else to say, please go ahead. Truth to tell, if I may say so, I cannot wait to assure you through my expertise that I did not copy anything and that I indeed know how to provide this expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think maybe we're working at cross purposes here. What I was suggesting to you was not that you stole and copied and published under your own name, but you had actually translated the work of other people and gave them credit for it but published in Serbian your translation of their work. Now, if that's incorrect, just tell me it's incorrect. You can say it in one word.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, that's undoable. There is the public, the scholarly public. There are re-appointments of university professors. Do you really think they would have kept me at university if I did things like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: People translate the work of other people all the time so it can be published in their language. There's nothing wrong with that. That's perfectly honourable. If one of your books had been translated by someone into English, they wouldn't have been stealing from you. They'd have been translating so it could be published in English. All I want to know is, did you write them or did you translate them from someone else? And you can just say, I wrote it myself, and then we're done with this.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not going to take your question as an insult. I'm going to tell you that I wrote all of this on my own and others copied from me. Out of my 28 books, several -- most of them or all of them were published three or four times, and the ones that you asked me about were published four times. I really don't know. This is something that does not go hand in hand with the ethics of a university professor as far as I'm concerned. Quite simply, I don't know how you came about such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were they ever published in any other language but Serbian, these two books?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. My doctorate on the polygraph and personal --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about the two books on graphology, graphoscopes. Those are the two books we're talking about. We're not talking about anything else. Were those two books ever translated into any other language?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: No, but had you allowed me to finish, I would have said where all those other books had been translated. But all right. These two had not been translated anywhere. They are originals, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. That's what I was trying to get to. We could have gotten there a long time ago. I want to ask you --

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- when you approach your work as an expert, and please understand I'm not making any effort here at all to make any accusations against you. I'm just trying to learn some things, and I'm not trying to insult you. And if you take that -- anything I say as an insult, I apologise. But when you approach this work --

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: May I respond in kind, then?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. Okay. Okay. Give me question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, as you approach your work as an expert, do you feel like you are independent and you make your judgements independent of the person that has asked you to do the work, or do you make an effort to tell that person what it is they want to hear? In other words, do you become an advocate for that side of the case?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never. I always write what my own findings are. I stand by that, and in the times of communism I had quite a few difficulties on account of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now we're going to get to what you actually did, and what you did were the things that Mr. Visnjic requested of you to do. That's a fair statement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. He is the one who commissioned my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if we put 3D 1130 up on the screen so you can see it, and go to page 7 in the colour B/C/S version. Now, if we could zoom in on line 82, please, just so we can see a little better. That's good enough. Now, what Mr. Visnjic asked you to do with regard to this document was to look at that line 82 and give him your opinion as to whether the person who entered the written information on that line was the same person who made changes in the rest of the document, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: No. Sir, I received this document with the following question being put to me, to establish whether any corrections had been made in hand in relation to the printed text, and I established that corrections were made by hand by two persons at that. Who these persons were, I don't know, and I'll let you know what the secret is, how I came to that conclusion. According to the way of writing, there is a swan-like way -- oh, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do what I ask you to do when I ask you a question. I'm not asking you for any more information than what I ask. Just listen to my question, and answer my question. We'll get where you're going, right. We will get there. Your expert report says that you were asked this question: Was the amendation made on page 7 in number 82, columns 4, 5, and 6, made by the same person who amended the figures in the other numbers in this document in columns 4, 5, 6, and 7? Now, that's what your report says. I asked you if that's what you were instructed to do, and you said no. Now, what is it? Isn't that exactly what you were asked to do? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: What is written here, at least in my copy, in line 82 on page 7, this was compiled by the person who made the other numerical changes. My understanding was that there were two persons involved, and I have no way of establishing who these persons were because then I'd have to go to the military archives and examine all the signatures and handwriting of all the persons who made changes. However, I thought that unusually so, there are two handwritings in this document in terms of the number 2, and I dwelled on that. I'm sorry if I disappointed you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Professor, it's not a question of whether you disappoint me or not, but you could help me a lot if you would listen to the question I ask you and answer that question instead of telling me something you want to tell me. Now, I mean, that would -- and I know you can do that. I know you can understand the language, you can understand the question, and you can understand what I'm asking you, and if you would just answer the question, we'd finish this in a reasonable amount of time. Otherwise, we're going to be here the rest of the day, and you'll get tired, and I'll get tired, and then we'll get snippy at each other, and who knows what'll happen next. But if we just try to do this in a reasonable way so you can answer the question that I ask you, we'll get through this. Okay?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: This time I would not like to use commonwealth -- or rather, common law terms such as reasonable. I'm going to resort to our own system. I see that two persons made these corrections. To this day, I don't know how Mladenovski who signed this writes the number 2 and how this other person writes and who writes in this swan-like way, so I cannot give you an answer. But I absolutely can respond if the Court deems this necessary. There were two persons who made changes on this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Tell me, what question of mine are you answering right now? What question of mine are you answering?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I -- please don't hold this against me. You put your questions to me, and I'll answer them, but I really don't want to be questioned in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you just answered a question I didn't ask you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, you've caused us a great deal of confusion --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then please be so kind as to put your question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, if you would just pay attention for a moment. You're causing us a great deal of confusion by claiming that what in the report you have said is not accurate, and that's what Mr. Ackerman is trying to clarify. You've set out the questions you were asked by Mr. Visnjic, and when Mr. Ackerman asked you just to confirm that as a prelude to something else, you've denied it. So you've caused confusion. Now, if you start from that point of view, bear in mind that if you don't listen very carefully to the question and answer only what you're asked, you are liable to cause confusion, which is not in the interests of Mr. Ojdanic. So let's proceed from there. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Professor, the second thing you were asked to do with regard to this document, and we need to look at the last page of it now. And there's some vertical handwriting down there in the bottom right-hand corner of this page. According to your report, you were asked if the person who wrote that note on the last page was the same person who made the changes we've been looking at in line 82. Now, all I'm asking you is if you understand that's what you were asked to do, not what you did. Just what you were asked to do.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic asked me to do the following. This text was received in the military archives by Mladenovski, and was it Mladenovski who changed columns 4, 5, 6, and 7? That's what he asked me about. And my answer to him was that what Mr. Mladenovski signed was what I compared to his notes in writing in hand that says not written and so on and so forth. So it is the same man who wrote this, but I did not establish whether he himself had made the changes except for what I said already, that there were two persons who made corrections. However, the handwritten text was provided by Mr. Mladenovski, the notes he made in hand, and finally his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. The third thing you were asked to do was to add up the number of documents in the columns and the number of pages in the columns and see if they matched the number on page 1 as to how many pages they were. Now, what part of your expertise makes you an expert on adding up numbers? That doesn't have anything to do with handwriting or document analysis, does it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a well-known method applied in arithmetic, adding.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Why didn't you tell Mr. Visnjic, Anybody can add, you don't need an expert to do that? Why did you agree to do this? You're this big fancy expert, and he's turning you into somebody that's adding up numbers.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, you know what? There is one thing that came up at least in our practice. There are people who come before a court of law and who are more familiar with weapons and, say, a Judge is very knowledgeable about weapons, but then he asks for an expert nevertheless. It is one thing if a lawyer indicates this adding, and it's a different thing if an expert indicates it. I think that is what it has to do with. I was not offended by that, that particular part, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, I agree with you because, you know, sometimes people will make mistakes in adding up numbers, and maybe he was just asking you to double-check this and see if the person who did that made a mistake, right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, you're probably going to check it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You can be certain that I already have.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I'm sure you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to go to another document. 3D 1131 is another document you were asked to look at, and I need to get it on the screen and look at the line that's number 248 in the Serbian version. It should be the next page.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can we just have the Serbian and the next page of it, please. I don't think we need to see the English. It's not relevant, so get rid of it, and just give me line 248 blown up. There we go. All right. What you were asked to do was to determine if the stamp 26.05.1999 in line 248 there was the same or identical to the 26.05.1999 date stamp in columns 250, 323, 325, 326, 327, 328, 329, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you asked to make a comparison between the handwriting that appears under number 2 in line 248 with the other handwriting in this document? You weren't, were you?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, in Yugoslavia court experts are used to the following. When they're involved in civil cases, then they --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're not answering my question --

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: -- they are directly related to what it was that they are supposed to do. I want to answer you. I really do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question was simple.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Oh, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You weren't asked to compare the handwriting in 248, line 2, with the other handwriting in the document, were you? You weren't asked to do that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: This is what the request was. Warrant Officer Dusan Mladenovski in the military archives, did he make changes in such and such columns and in terms of the signature on the last page? I admit that apart from that request I established that Mladenovski made written corrections in the document, and I identified them. As far as I've been informed, Mr. Mladenovski testified here and admitted that, so that has been a source of satisfaction for me, the fact that I said something that was correct although I didn't even know him. So that is what I have to say in relation to Mladenovski's signature. Could you just tell me this other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, that's absolutely nothing to do with the question you've just been asked. There's a limit to the Court's patience on this. We have a very large agenda of what to get through this a case as gross as this, so please, concentrate on the question. It's a very simple one. Were you asked to compare the handwriting in the second line of 248 with the other writing in other parts of that document? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I need to learn how you do that, Judge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the first time in this expertise that it seems to be detrimental if I establish more than originally requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, yesterday we got a supplement, and it was up on the screen here, all the numbers in colour that we saw earlier.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know what I'm talking about --

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Numerator, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, was this analysis requested by Mr. Visnjic, or is this just something you decided to do on your own?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Let me just have a look at the request. In the request, it says that the date of the 26th of May, 1999, in columns 248 -- or rather, in column 248, is what is requested and then the same date, and then the rest is listed. So it was my understanding that, yes, that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that was part of what you were asked to do?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: It was my understanding of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to ask you about your visit to the archives. When did you and Mr. Visnjic go to the archives and look at these documents? When? The only question I'm asking you is when.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I think it was in December, last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: December of 2007?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you said something in your direct that you looked at them under very vigilant eyes. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, you know what it's like. It's this very long room. The way in which the originals are brought in is very complicated. So then I looked this up in the books, and then I isolated this, and I looked at the book. All the time next to me there were, say, four or five employees of the archives, and then there was Visnjic, and I don't know. Somebody else, too, perhaps. So in a way, I isolated myself in thoughts from them, jotted this down, and decided that I would make my basic findings once I received the copies. However, as I was looking at the originals, I was looking for possible traces of scanning or some other technique of dealing with documents. That was my objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the question really was was what do you mean by vigilant eyes, and you told us that there were four or five people there watching you. So I take it if you had wanted to make some kind of a change in one of these original documents, you wouldn't have been able to get by with it. They would have caught you doing it, right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't do such a thing, would I?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you would have gotten caught if you tried, wouldn't you? I know you wouldn't do such a thing, but if you tried they would have seen you doing it, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I am not stopped from committing a crime by the possibility of somebody seeing me committing a crime. I have devoted my entire life to things like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you have any of your instruments with you when you went to the archive to use to examine these documents, or did you just visually examine them?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: First of all, as an expert, my examinations are not simple. I did not have an apparatus next to me, and I devoted --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: -- attention to the possibility of scanning or some kind of other change, and that can be seen only on the back of the original document because of the relief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question is, did you have any instruments with you or not? I think your answer is, no, you didn't, right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, it's a bit ridiculous. With all due respect, and I really am sorry because of the Judges, but I'm not a man who strolls about and does this and that. When I look at documents, there is always an objective involved. The first time I went there was whether I could see what is visible on copies and originally whether I could establish whether the documents had been scanned or not. That has to be determined on the basis of the original. I'm sorry if I took up too much time answering.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm told it might be break time, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't even, for example, carry a magnifying glass with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had a pocket magnifying glass; however, Your Honour, sir, when an expert in graphology gets an object and if he's just exploring it initially, he is looking at the relief and looking at the light as it falls on the document. I had a pocket magnifying glass, but that didn't really mean anything. It just meant that I could rely on the copies once I received; however, what I established was that although today it is possible to tamper with documents electronically, these had not been tampered with. My stereomicroscope weighs 60 kilogrammes, and I don't carry that around. I brought a photograph of that device if you wish to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I think we can leave it to the counsel -- we can leave it to counsel to ask any necessary questions about the equipment. We need to have a break at this stage, Professor. It's routine in our proceedings. That break will be for 20 minutes. While we have the break, could you please leave the courtroom with the usher, and we will see you again at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the 1996 Rules of Service have arrived; they're in the hands of your assistants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We need to have 3D 1130 put back on the screen, and just the Serbian version, please. We don't need the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Professor, when did you first meet with or talk with Mladenovski?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know Mladenovski, and I've never met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you figure out some way to get handwriting exemplars from him without talking to him?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, in the document itself, the one that I analysed, I found his notes and then signature at the end. And then when I heard that he accepted it here and admitted it here, I was quite content.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well -- but, before you'd heard that he accepted it here, you had no idea that that was his writing, did you, because you hadn't compared it with anything?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In over 90 per cent of the cases when those giving the last will are dead, I establish the authenticity of last wills by comparing the signatures in documents presented to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm just guessing, but in my experience with people who do the work that you do, I suspect that when you lecture about this and in the book that you wrote or in the books that you wrote, whatever you've done in that regard, that one of the things that you have emphasized is the necessity of getting detailed handwriting exemplars if you're going to compare handwriting to an unknown sample. You've done that, haven't you? You've said that's important, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the basic rule; however, in certain cases when you have a number of possibilities of making conclusions based on available documents and if it is difficult to obtain handwriting samples from all of the employees, in this particular case I had sufficient evidence and sufficient skill so that it wasn't necessary for me to explore the subject further than this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't know when any of the handwritten imprints on this document were made, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, the conclusion you drew with regard to this document was that - and we could go to page 7, please - was that a different person made these changes in line 82 from who had made changes in other parts of the document, and I think I'm being fair to you when I say that you based your decision primarily on the way the number 2 is shaped. You said that the number 2 in that line 82 has what you called a swan's neck termination, and if you look at other number 2s written in the document, they have what you called a level termination. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And, for instance, if we look at line 84 there, we see the 2s there that have those, you know, kind of straight lines coming out the back of them, right, and that's the level termination you're talking about, true?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if we looked at line 79, just go up just a tad, we'd also see a 2 there with a -- what you call a level termination?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, because what I described as a swan-like figure 2 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: She wants you to repeat your answer, so say it again, what you described as a swan-like 2 or something.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In this document, there are just several. Most of them have a flat termination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the first page of this document, please, and go to the bottom of the page, line 6. Line 6, please. Try to blow up line 6 there so we can see the 2 there really good. There we go. Is that a swan's-neck termination, there? It's not a flat termination, is it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: No. A swan-neck's termination pertains to the head and the neck, if I may say so. The termination is flat in this particular case, and it's not extended as it normally should be as in column 1 because figures 1 and 7 follow. When people write in these columns, they tend to amend their handwriting because there's no sufficient space. As an example, one never analyses a signature on a pay stub because there's not enough room in the column to put a signature there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Let's go look at -- this does have a little loop there where the bottom of that 2 is made that we don't see on these other level terminations that you were showing us. But let's go to another one. Let's go to line 29, and I think that's on page 3. We'll just have to check. Yeah, it's on page 3 about two-thirds of the way down. Now, look at that 2 there. That's a definite swan's neck, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for accepting this term.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. It's a good term. I like it. And so we can conclude that the person who made that 2 in line 29 is the same person who made the changes in line 84 that we were looking at -- 82 that we were looking at earlier, can't we?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's look at line 93, and we'll find that over on page -- that's on page 7, and it's at the very bottom.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. In this case here, there is a rudimentary swan form there, if I may say so. Your Honour, may I make a comment, something very briefly, that will clarify certain things. I did not count the instances of one number 2 and the other number 2; I simply took the figure 2 as a prominent one to confirm my thesis that two people made corrections. I didn't analyse this further. I believed that it was up to the Court to decide whether it was important or not, and if so, that it could be further analysed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, the other thing you did with regard to this document is you looked at that handwriting on the last page where it's signed with the name of Mladenovski. Now, in that handwriting on the last page, there aren't any numbers, are there?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No numbers in that handwriting?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I didn't analyse the numbers. I analysed something else, and I wrote that down. I analysed letters, J, K, and so on. At any rate, I was certain that there was sufficient, both general and individual features, in this group, which turned out to be correct, and I wrote this accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next document, then, 1131. And again, we only need the Serbian. We don't need English. Were you ever in the room at the General Staff Supreme Command where documents were being entered into this log-book in 1999? Were you ever there?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So of your own knowledge, at least, you have no knowledge as to whether or not the people working at that location and in that room were actually entering every document in the log-book that they were receiving, do you? You don't know that they were being totally accurate about that, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to anybody who was there at the time, who was working there at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I think that the person who was in charge there, he wore a camouflage uniform, and he addressed me as Professor Aleksic, and I thought that he knew me from the law school because we had a lot of people from the military attending our law school. However, I didn't introduce myself to him because it wasn't the right time, and I was too busy analysing what I have just described to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You didn't ask him any questions about what went on there in 1999, I take it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you have no idea how many different date stamps they had there in 1999 that they were using, do you? As far as you know, they could have had ten?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know what methods are used in working with military documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's not my question. You don't know --

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: However, I can identify and recognise -- I know it's not your question, but I feel the need to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, why don't you answer my question?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I've answered your question. I have none. I don't know. I didn't do anything. I didn't do any work there, and I'm not interested in that. Why would I at this age study the methods of using stamps in the military archives? I would not accept such an assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think if I was going to come and sit in front of a Court under oath and tell Judges conclusions that I've drawn from looking at date stamps on a document, I would want to know whether there was more than one date stamp available to the people that did it. That makes sense, doesn't it? That's why you would want to know that. Do you know how many ink-pads they had?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: It's obvious that you are more diligent and better than I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know how many ink-pads they had there at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You made conclusions about ink colours without knowing how many ink-pads they had there and what colours they were, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're fully right, but bear in mind the document that I provided. There you can see how calibrated 2s differ from each other, both in terms of calibre and colour, and that's sufficient for me. At that point of time, it was sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's sufficient to show they were made by a different date stamp using a different stamp-pad. That's all that shows, isn't it? It doesn't show anything else. Any other conclusion you made is one as an advocate, not as an expert.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you agree that I added there that the calibre of figure 2 was greater and that the location, the original location, of figure 2 in the numerator was disturbed. I think that's of importance to the Court, perhaps even to you, but definitely to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree. That would be important if you knew what kind of stamp-pads they had and what kind of numerators they were using, what kind of equipment they were using, but you didn't know any of that. You're just assuming that kind of thing, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: No, that's not speculation. That's my claim. It is my position that the numerator was predated or antedated and that when the numbers were moved around, a different ink-pad was used, and the figures did not go back to their original position. I think that that's clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I need the usher to come see me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to have the usher show you something and ask you if you know what it is.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I hope that you're not testing my skill again. This is the numerator, and here the figures can be moved either using a needle or using the button on the side, depending on the numerator. This is a more modern type. The Chinese produce them nowadays.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, that's the kind of numerator you had in mind when you were writing this report, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Numerators come in different shapes, but the principle is the same. The numbers are rolled around and adjusted. Today, I finished stamping 26, and starting tomorrow, I will stamp 27, and if I need some other date, then I can look for numbers 23 and 24 in the archives. If I use an inadequate numerator, then everybody will know that I did it afterwards. I did it subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, did you go back to the archives and look at this document after December?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: No, and they wouldn't have let me in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it's also true, isn't it, that in your original report in this case you said nothing about a difference in colour of those stamps?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. I said at the outset that I first analysed the dots and provided explanation, but now just before coming here I went to see people at the police who gave me a special piece of equipment which enabled me to establish this additional feature, which I thought would be of assistance to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Looking at copies not the originals, right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Correct, but one cannot obtain originals from the military at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you know that the ink you were looking at on the copies was not ink from a stamp-pad but ink from a copy machine. So you're comparing ink colours from a copy machine and translating that into ink colours from a stamp-pad. I don't think that works, does it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You know what, it is not my profession to use spectrum analysis of colour and so on. My profession was of assistance to point to a suspicious piece of information here. One can apply spectrum analysis to analyse colour and so on, but at this point in time I thought that this was sufficient because this is an official archive and not a place where some local, low-level clerks perhaps used inadequate methods when keeping books.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know that this is a serious court of law where you're expected to do what scientifically you should do, and you're in here telling us you've compared colours from a copy machine, and that makes some sense to you, and that's something this Court should draw conclusions from? Is that what you're saying? I thought you would flunk any student that'd do what you did.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I have to tell you that I was an expert before this Court at least in one other case if not more cases, and fortunately, I did not come across such objections as yours, and I leave it up to your conscience to draw your own conclusions. I know that this is a serious court. I have a great deal of respect for it, even though this court deals with numerous crimes committed by people in my country.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I want to look now at that document you created recently that has all the 26.05s on it. I think it maybe got an IC number, did it, or do we have to put it back on the ELMO or what? If we can get it where we can see all eight numbers at once. Zoom out a little bit. That's seven. There's one more down there, I think, isn't there? Number 8 -- no, that's all. Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank goodness for the expert in arithmetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you make an issue out of the 2s that are in the first two lines, that they're, you know, big, bold, and thick, and 62 in the first line. If you go down to the next-to-the-last line, look at that 2. That one's kind of big and thick, too, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh, it isn't. Okay. Look at --

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- 326 and 327. The 2 is thicker in 326 than it is in 327, isn't it? And why is that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
