utterances.text: It's because of the ink-pad and the material underneath. However, if I dare use this term again - I see that you like my terms - they are Gullivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I like that one. Let's look at 325. Look at the 9s in 325, especially that last 9. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: 9 was not a subject of expertise because there was no reason for that. Everything is 1999 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not asking you --

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: The problem is only in the first part of the date --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, I know I'm answering -- I mean, I'm answering to the illogical nature of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the Judges will decide whether I'm being logical or not. Look at 325 and the 9s in there, and compare that with the 9s down in 327. They're much thicker and heavier, aren't they? How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I explain it by the fact that the first two 2s are really Gullivers compared to all of the others. Everything else in the stamp varies in terms of thickness; however, that is not relevant for our conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you would probably agree with me, because otherwise we've got a problem here, that the way the impression looks depends on how the stamp is used. So if, for instance, you ink it and press straight down, you get one kind of impression. If you ink it and roll it on, you're going to get a different kind of impression. If you put more force on the left side than the right side, you'll get another different kind of impression. It depends on how you're using the stamp, not necessarily on the stamp itself, what the impression is going to look like, right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You are quite right. However, you can roll it, press it, do whatever you want, but you cannot get this kind of a gigantic 2. I want to draw your attention to another thing now that we're talking about this. Since this 2 was moved at a later stage, it did not fall in its place, so to speak, and that can be seen very nicely. I thought about that a lot, whether the stamping took place twice along with the move because it seems that the second 2 was better put. Now, whether that had to do with additional activity -- well, but then that would just be story-telling. However, this is the way it is. As you put it, an expert would know that, and this is an enormous difference that gives me a certainty that I believe somebody like Mladenovski will admit to, and then you will probably forget about your objections in respect of my expert knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mladenovski had nothing to do with this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've used two expressions here, which I would be helped by you clarifying. You talked about a giant 2 -- a gigantic 2. What are you referring to as a gigantic 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, the calibre; and then secondly, this line that you can see up here that is drawn up here and then the one down here, the white one, show --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll need to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that the positions were moved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll need to point these out. It's the expression "gigantic." Gigantic is to do with size, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what do you mean by gigantic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, over here. Right. This is the first one, the first number 2, and may I jump to the other 2s here now. Already here, you see that it's different. There can be an augmented 2, as Mr. Ackerman said, through surface, different kind of using the ink-pad, and so on. However, the difference is so big here that my assertion is that it was antedated. Look at these two 2s. You'll see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: By gigantic, do you mean thicker?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Calibre, the calibre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. When you go up here from -- when you draw this line from the top of the 2, it goes down and touches the 9s; however, that's not the case with the other numbers. All things considered, the calibre tells us here that this is not an effective manipulation but of another numerator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, you referred a moment ago to a white line. Which white line were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Down here, down here. Do you see it here, and then here as well. Underneath every number, there are white lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Now, you also used an expression, calling something Gullivers, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number 2. Take the last one, for instance, where there is this thin 2 and then the one up here. It really does look as if it were its uncle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 2 down here in the last line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, it's the word that's concerning me. I'm not following this. Is the word you're using Gulliver?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes, yes. I studied that a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And how does that have a bearing on the shape or size of these numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. If I can use the phrase, it looks like a man who weighs 150 kilogrammes and another man that weighs 50 kilogrammes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it's a difference that you're talking about. Now, can I just briefly have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Calibre, calibre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But let me ask the usher to bring over the document from the ELMO, please. Now, this is -- as I understood it, this was a colour copy of 3D 1148, page 3, but 3D 1148 has eight rows of 26.05.1999, and this one has only seven.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we have that clarified by someone who knows about these things? It would appear the bottom one from column 329 is missing from the colour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 329. I have it here. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you shall have this one back, and it's a matter for Mr. Visnjic to try to clarify, but it's causing further confusion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please take this. [In English] That's right, you have -- [Interpretation] This document has all the numbers. With your permission, perhaps the usher could take it to you. Seven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the source of the one that became the IC number? Was it Mr. Hannis or was it -- it wasn't. What was the source of that coloured copy, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, now I really don't know who gave you a copy: Was it Mr. Hannis, or was it me? I have a copy here with eight, eight. This is probably a document where the last page had not been printed. That's the only comment I can make. I have another copy with eight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but the evidence has been given on the basis of a document with seven on it, and that will continue to be the case for our assessment. That's the way the evidence has been presented. As long as you know the position, you can take steps to try to deal with it if necessary in re-examination. Please continue, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the one we have on the screen now, Your Honour, is a new one with eight --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no -- unless you want it and want to give it a new number, we should go back to the one we had and were working on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's totally out of focus. If it can get in focus, it might be more useful because I thought -- I thought we had a document with eight numbers. That's what I had. I was kind of surprised when it came up with seven. I thought maybe it was my inability to add. I don't know if we can get it in better focus. That's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The -- Professor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are we now moving to this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, we can -- I'd like -- let's put the old one back -- let's put the old one back with seven since we were using it. It doesn't make any difference. It works just as well for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Professor, these stamps that these dates are made out of -- stamped on there with are made out of rubber like the one I just showed you. And I know you will agree with me that the more pressure you put on a rubber number the bigger it gets; it expands, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, but this involves an enormous expansion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if you push hard, it will expand, and if you just touch it lightly, it will hold its original shape, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, you're not quite correct because there is a limit to this explanation, and this goes beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Look at all the 05s here. All the 05s that we see here are nearly identical. The first one's a little darker, might be an ink problem, but the rest of them are all identical, aren't they, or nearly so?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. The month and 1999 is obviously the log from that period; however, the 2 is the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, so if somebody had that stamp that's made out of rubber and made that top stamp by pushing down real hard on the left side, that would enlarge the 2 and the 6, leave the 5 and the 1999 looking like all the rest of them look, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I don't think you're right. The 2 comes from a different type of numerator. You said yourself that in big archives there are certainly countless numerators, whereas this is a different one that wasn't used for the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, and you might be right about that. I'll hand that to you. And if somebody used a different numerator --

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- if somebody used a different numerator to enter that date, it doesn't mean it was antedated. It just means they used a different numerator. So your conclusion about antedating holds no water at all, does it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: That's what you think, but I'll tell you how it does hold water. First of all, the numerator -- I mean, the question is, why would a different numerator be used? Why would a different --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... two different people are entering the documents in the log. That's one reason it could happen that way, or if the same person is doing it and just picks up a different numerator. There's a lot of documents going through there, a lot of them being logged on the same day. They're busy.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me how you'd explain that only those two numbers do not match? And as far as I know --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to show you in a minute. Trust me, I'll show you. I want to know if -- this is something I found that's written. I want to know if you agree with this statement that's written here. "The date stamp is not a stable device. It's a mechanically unstable item which is not appropriate at all for exact expert analysis on the basis of which someone could give an opinion with 100 per cent certainty." Do you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: No, because this involves extreme magnitude that shows a completely different picture rather than a mistake in manipulation. If you wish, you can add to that that subsequent movement of the dial, either with a needle or in another way, the number can never fall into the same place, the number that's being changed. That is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: A subsequent movement doesn't change its size, does it? A subsequent movement doesn't make the 2 bigger?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: It will if a different calibre of numerator was taken. For example, the one that you showed me just now, your numerator, for an archive it can be of tiny dimensions. There's a lot of work that has to be done during the course of a day, so there's a big difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want you to watch what I'm going to do. Watch me. I've got the numerator in my hand. This is a red ink-pad, okay? I've touched it to the ink-pad, and I've put it on the page. I've touched it to the ink-pad, and I've put it on the page. I've touched it to the ink-pad, and this time I'm going to put a lot of pressure on the left side, 2, and touch it to the page. And this time, I'm going to do that again. I'll ask the usher to show you this. Put it on the ELMO. Now, this is all the same numerator and the same ink-pad, but look at that third 2 down there. Is that what you would call one of those gigantic 2s?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: First of all, let me answer that question. No. No, because look at this. The third one is blurred, smeared, and this one here is clear. Then the upper one was not printed right, but you have general characteristics here that are identical. So any expert would say that it is the same numerator. The smear is something for which the person doing this is to be blamed. Now look at this here. Look, if you can see it now -- just a moment, please. Let's try to do it this way. Look at this. Look at this -- oh, you can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Bring that paper back to me a minute because I did make a mistake when I smeared it.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: With pleasure. So I do know how to establish something, don't I?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Take it back now. What I did was push down real hard on the left side again, and I think you'll see that it made the 2 bigger than the other 2s, still a bit of a smear but not as much, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: This number 2 is smeared, sir, Mr. Ackerman. And secondly, do you notice that the base did not change in terms of its dimensions. Your Honour, I said what I had to say. I'm sorry that this has not reached its destination, but I leave that to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you mean by saying the base did not change in terms of its dimensions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have a look at this down here, the third one, the third one that Mr. Ackerman said that he pressed hard on purpose to the left and therefore smeared it. Do you see it? It's quite different. This is an artificial increase, but this is a different numerator altogether. It's not the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm asking you what you meant by saying the base did not change in terms of its dimension. It looks --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The base of this number 2 that Mr. Ackerman, as he says himself, pressed to the left down here. You see that the ink moved, but still the number 2 is thin, nevertheless, at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That needs an IC number, I guess --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But before you -- and I don't see that. It seems to me that the 2 is clearly fatter at the bottom. I'm obviously not looking at the same thing as you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me? Are you addressing this question to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not understanding what you mean by saying that the dimension at the base is the same.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may call for your patience a bit more. Practically if somebody looks at this, the dimensions are more or less the same. However, any expert would tell you that this third number is actually something that has to do with a lack of concentration or attention, but the 8s and everything else are the same, the 9s too. But if you look at this number 2, it has a different position, a different slant, and its size is considerably different, whereas here, in spite of Mr. Ackerman's effort, I think that it would be no use to him if he tried to use that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You have lost me on this. If you look at 3D -- sorry, IC 19 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you look at your original, IC196, with the 26.05 on it, the top two 2s are just the same -- the bottom of them's just the same as the others only a bit fatter, and that seems to me to be what's on the one that you've just been shown. Am I missing -- am I misunderstanding it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, if I may say so, the 2 has a different material on which it was put and what shows that this was done subsequently; and secondly, it has to do with a different machine that leaves a different imprint. You cannot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on. Which are you talking about at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first two big 2s, not Mr. Ackerman's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, I'm not asking you about them. I'm asking you about the other one. Put them side by side on the ELMO, please, and come out so that we can see it all clearly. Now, if you look at the last of these 2s on the right-hand side, the red one, 26 and then the word -- followed by the word "Mei," and if you look at the third one, are you telling me that the bottom line of these 2s is the same dimension as the bottom line of the other three on that list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, sir, if an expert were to look at only these five stamps made by Mr. Ackerman, not a single one would tell you that it's not the same one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not my question, Professor --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- it would be described to manipulation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understood that, but that's not my question. You made a very clear statement that the dimensions of the bases of the 2s were identical, and I just don't understand that statement, and that's what I'm trying to clarify because to me they look different. Now, what is it that makes you say that the bases of these 2s are the same as the other three 2s when they plainly are fatter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I have to say to you - you will probably agree with me - that the first and second one from the top -- stamps from the top are practically the same for the most part. The third one is smeared, and obviously it shows that there was a mistake in terms of manipulation. The fourth stamp, one, two, three, four, the fourth one is a normal one. I mean normal in the sense of what was expected of the numerator, the device. And the fifth one, again, in terms of the original position and general characteristics, we see that it comes from the same device except that in case of the 2 the blanks are filled; however, it doesn't make it a gigantic 2 yet again. Sorry, I don't seem to be responding properly. I hope that I have given an answer to what you had asked me about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you haven't answered my question, but I think we've exhausted it. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Professor, I want to read you your opinion on your supplemental information sheet. You say this: "In the log-book in question, the traces of the date 26.05.1999 in columns 248 and 250 differ from the traces of the same date in columns 323, 268, 325, 326, 327, 328, and 329," and all of us looking at that can agree that they differ. But then you take this leap: "Which indicates counterfeiting, that is that the dates in columns 248 and 250 was not printed on the same day when the dates in the other said columns were printed." Now, as I understand your testimony, and you tell me if I'm wrong, what you claim happened here was that the 2 on the stamp was moved to subsequent numbers and then later some day moved back to that 2, and you couldn't ever get it back the same way so that when you made a stamp with that 2 the second time, it's this big fat stamp that you see in 248 and 250. Now, is that the basis of your conclusion? Is that what you're making this broad conclusion on, on that kind of testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You're fully right. This first imprint and the second one were made with the same numerator. However, this first one, in it the number 2 has a somewhat different position than in the other one. I do not have sufficient elements to claim that this figure 2 was moved twice; however, I have sufficient elements for saying that these 2s come from different stamps and are not of the same date as the others in the document. How am I making this conclusion? I'm making it because all numbers have a similar shape except in the first two imprints. I don't know whether this is sufficient explanation or not for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if we have an interpretation problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you like me to repeat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've been translated into English as saying that these 2s come from different stamps, and that needs to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The first two 2s, or rather, that entire imprint, they come from a different numerator. Now, whether they changed the dates twice, I wouldn't be able to say, but they were definitely changed, and they were stamped separately from the others, which created this prominent difference in calibre. This is what gives me the basis for claiming what I have claimed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, I have -- I have misunderstood you all along then. I did not understand we were talking about two separate pieces of equipment being used here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that just by looking at it without a looking-glass, just using a naked eye, one can tell that these two imprints differ from the other ones, and this came about because a different numerator was used, and in the first two cases the imprint was made that way. It is possible that the imprint was made once and that the 2 was moved and then stamped again, but I can't go as far as to actually claim that. It is clear, however, that it is not consistent with other numerators, and, Your Honours, it seems to me that this is quite clear just by looking at this with the naked eye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, Professor, I have a question just to clarify my own thoughts. I would request you to help me in this respect. Now, you are firm on this that two numerators were used. Okay. But could they have been used on the same date? How are you getting the conclusion with respect to the use of different numerators on different dates? Now, that I'm not able to understand. I'm sorry for that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the first and the second imprint come from a different numerator as compared to the rest, six or seven, of them; that's clear. And in the first one and in the second one, you can see that between themselves they differ. First of all, in the position of figure 2 in its thickness, and one would need a very sophisticated and labour-intensive method to establish whether this has been changed twice. At this point in time, however, I can confirm that the first and the second numerator is of a different kind than in the rest of those imprints and that its use in this particular document was something that pointed me in the direction of predating. In addition to this, there are also dots after 6 and 5. If you look at these clear, uncontested imprints, then one can see that these dots are very close to the imprint line in all of these cases except in the first two imprints where there is a distance between the imprint line and the dot, and this is what prompted me to do this other analysis and present it to you. I regret that I'm not convincing enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm just seeking a clarification, but kindly tell me, how do you say that this was antedated? I mean, what are the basis? I mean, there could be two numerators used on the same date. If you could help me knowing this, that would be very useful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know, it is easy to recognise an instrument, a type and other features, and this is what I used to draw my conclusion. Please bear in mind one thing, that this list that was created came from our basic list and compiled that way just to draw your attention to this. Otherwise, the order in the document itself is quite different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but, Professor, you're being asked why you say they could not both have been done on the same day. The fact that they are different does not mean that they were done on different days. Now, what is your reason for saying they were done on different days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that only the head of the institution in charge of this could give you an answer to that. I can't give you an answer. They all know each other. They recognise each other's stamps, and they know these things; however, I can't gain access to that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: So therefore, it is possible that two numerators may have been used on the same date. What would you say on that? And there was a question whether you were good enough in checking the number of numerators available with the repository of this, which of course was not done, and now we have to then guess what it could be. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know what? I can't know that fact, how many numerators there were. Everything that one wanted to obtain in that archives had to be made -- requested in writing, and then permission had to be sought, and one had to wait for, like, a month. However, it is normal to use a numerator if one works in the archives, and then if another one is used on the following day, then it's quite clear why it was done. And here it seems that there were just a total of two numerators, and one should look into the issue of which documents were covered by this, if I may call it, gigantic numerator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Now, as I see these lines, because of which you were able to distinguish between the sizes of the -- of the digits, I find these going slanting one way or going slanting the other way. What is the scientific method then used? Because these lines do not appear facsimile. These appear different, some going in a tangent, some going a little different. That confuses me, and may I request you to kindly, because of your learning, explain this position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I worked with a stereomicroscope, Olympus, with a mobile head, and that kind of equipment gives the best results in these situations. I can give you this picture of -- the photograph of the Olympus. However, I wasn't able to take this equipment to the archives because it weighs between 45 and 60 kilos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: So where did you draw these lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I drew the line at the top, the first one. I connected the 2 and the tops of the 9s. The line at the bottom is less slanted. You see that the angle is less sharp, and then in the third instance you see that these lines connecting 2 and 999, there's very little discrepancy there. As for the dots after 6 and after 5, they're in a way different, whereas with the rest of the imprints, all these dots are parallel, and they touch the line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And, learned Professor, then you got the impression that there was rotation on the -- on that instrument, is it, is it because of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because the figure 2 did not go back to its original position, and this -- in this entire sample, regardless of the size, the 2 is always in the same location and does not oscillate, except in the case of these two, which points me in the direction of a subsequent imprint. Thank you for your questions. I think that you help me be more clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I hope we're nearing the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We might be, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there's a limit to the time that can be spent on this one subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Professor, the Judge wants me to hurry up, and I'm going to, but I need your cooperation in that regard. In your original report, the basis for your conclusion was that the one numerator had been changed to new dates, and then at some later date taken back to the 26th of May and stamped that way, and you said that's why the 2 is bigger, because it didn't get put back in the same place. Now, today you've decided to change that testimony and say that it was two different numerators that made these stamps. I'm going to give you an opportunity that I probably shouldn't give you, but I will. I'm going to give you an opportunity to withdraw from your opinion the language which says -- which indicates counterfeiting that the dates in the columns were not printed on the same day when the dates in the other columns were printed. I'm going to give you a chance to withdraw that opinion because it's clearly wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you like to withdraw it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, before we do this, Mr. Ackerman, I don't -- unless I'm again misunderstanding it, I don't think you've presented the position accurately. Because now that I read the original report in the light of the recent exchange, it does say on page 5: "It may be concluded from this that the stamp which was used for columns 323," et cetera, "was different from the date stamp used in column 248." Now, I agree, I thought having reading the supplementary information sheet that that in fact meant the stamp had been changed in some way in its format, but that seems to be presupposing originally two stamps, and then the confusion I think comes in in the second report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I thought the supplemental was replacing the original in that regard. Maybe I was wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, but you've put them the wrong way around, I think. That's all I'm saying, or have I -- just a second. In your original report, you say your conclusion was that one numerator had been changed. So you're regarding the original report as the supplemental information sheet because we've got on the second page of it, we go into the detail about the difference between 248 and 250, and the conclusion that is then drawn about counterfeiting and the dates is another leap forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the original report says that the date stamp to make the 248 and 250 was a different stamp from the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then the supplement says, No, that's not what it was, it was because this was moved and then brought back, and that's how I conclude that it was made after the fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what I thought it said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think that's what he was saying. And now I'm giving him a chance to simply withdraw his conclusion that what you see in front of us indicates counterfeiting, and I don't know if he wants to do that or not, but I invite him to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's your answer to that, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that you're fully right, that this supplement derogates the initial information. As for Mr. Ackerman's gift, I cannot accept it because you know that old proverb: Fear of the Greeks even when bringing gifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I know that you are highly trained and highly skilled, at least that's what you tell us. And everybody in the courtroom that's looking at this document can see that the 2s in the first two lines there are different from the rest of the 2s, so nobody's arguing with you about that. Nobody. What nobody can understand is how the fact that those 2s are larger than the other 2s means that they weren't put there on the 26th of May. That's a leap that no one understands and that I suggest to you you simply cannot make. Now, that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: No, I don't understand that. I'm trying to say this. What you have on the screens right now on the left has been cut out in order to be shown here, but if you look at the original document with these stamps, you will see that this fat figures of 2 and 6 have been imprinted in several places, in two places, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know, I think we can ask you this question 25 times here today, and we're going to get the same nonsense answer from you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The matter's been exhausted, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I now want to look at 3D 1131 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we need an IC number for the red-stamped document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh, we need an IC number for that --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC 197, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I've got, like, one or two more questions, Judge, and I'm done. 3D 1131, please. Just the Serbian version. We don't need the English. The second page, please. And I just want to blow up the top part of that document, the first two columns, 247, 248. That's probably as good as we're going to be able to get.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Professor, I want you to look at line 248, the second entry there. Look at the 872 and the 1, okay?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You said 248. What do you want me to look at there?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The line 2, column -- I can't read that -- column 6 --

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, 28th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. There's an 872, and then there's some other numbers and a 1. Those are the numbers I want you to concentrate on. Do you see them?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I see 248. Do you want me to discuss that first?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I don't want you to discuss that at all. I want you to go to the second entry in 248, and go over to column 6, and you should see handwritten 872 --

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 872-94/1-2. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Go straight above that, and you see an 872-137/1. Now, isn't it the case that the person who wrote the 872 in 248 is the same person who wrote it in 247? It's the same writing, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: It is very difficult to say because it is a limited space. All I can say for a fact is that this is a different writing implement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's see if we can blow up those two numbers more and get kind of tight in on that part of the thing so you can see them better. Look at how distinctive that 1 is. That 1 is made in a distinctive way, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You mean 153 or at the top?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Those 1s -- in both those boxes, the 1s are very, very distinctive. They've got a little tail there toward the bottom. You see them?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the 872 look virtually identical, don't they?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: 872. Where have you seen that? What date is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you looking at the screen? It's right in front of you under number 6. Don't you see the two 872s there?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Will you please show it. Point it to me, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, look at your screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am. 872-94/1-2. What do you want me to do with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you go above that, you'll see 872-137/1 at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same person wrote this. You mean column 6, the first entry, 872, and then the second 872 under the 26th of May. This was written by the same person, and 1 and 2 are quite prominent. I did not analyse this, but I can look at it now, and most likely this was done by the same person. Now, what's the purpose of this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't need to know. I'm through asking you questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just to end on consensus. Professor, we need to have another break at this stage --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have the last one remaining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just leave everything in front of you there. We have to have a break now for half an hour. Again, would you leave the courtroom with the usher, please, and we will see you again at five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, you'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, I just have a handful of questions for you, really. One of the first ones I had was at page 8, line 15, today. You were talking about when you went to the archives with Mr. Visnjic and looked at the documents, and one of the things you were looking for was to see whether or not any of the originals had been scanned, and you talked about the importance of looking at the back page of the original. Can you explain to me what that's for, why you do that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, let me tell you, scanning considerably imperilled my profession. You get a handwriting that is completely authentic; however, there are about eight ways of establishing whether the document had been scanned. That can be done by examining the original and the back side of the original document. Light is cast on the document. You look at a testament, a last will, and you look at the front page, and then on the other side you look at the back side, and then say the lady leaving, this is her last will and testament wrote flatly, now, why was that -- well, anyway, I'm just giving you an example. Never mind. I have to be very careful. I do take colour photocopies, but before that I have to establish that I'm working on the basis of originals that were copied in colour. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Hannis, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you looking at the document to see if what you have is a scanned copy? Is that what you're trying to check for? You'll have to answer out loud.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Scanning is one of these forms. There have been many improvements, especially now that there are electronic signatures in banks and elsewhere, so that has to be ruled out. There are eight ways of doing that. I don't want really want to educate you about that now, but then there is relief, and then there is -- if you look at the edges, there are imperceptible lines when a document is scanned and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you able to satisfy yourself that the documents you looked at in the archives were originals rather than scanned copies?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Hannis, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I had some questions about the numerator, but I think that's been covered. You did talk about Exhibit 3D 1130. If we could have that on the screen, please. Mr. Ackerman was asking you about some of the handwritten number 2s or numeral 2s, and at page 39 of the transcript today at --

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- at line 6, Mr. Ackerman asked you a question, and in your answer you said that you could -- "we can conclude that the person who made that 2 in line number 29" -- I think we have to go to page 2 or 3 of this document to get line 29. If you'll bear with me for a moment, Professor, while we pull that up.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. You agree with Mr. Ackerman that that appeared to be one of what you referred to as a swan's-neck ending on the numeral 2. And you said: "So we can conclude that the person who made that 2 in line 29 is the same person who made the changes in line 84 that we were looking at -- 82 that we were looking at earlier, can't we?" And you said yes to that question. I'm asking you, is it your opinion that just by looking at that one number you're able to say that the same person wrote that number in line 29, that same person also wrote the number that you see in line 82. If we could go to that page in this document.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Honourable Prosecutor, before we see this, let me say something else. I said that with a bit of reservation, if I may remind you. When people fill out very small questionnaires, forms, they usually split the numbers up. So as for handwriting expertise in little boxes in documents, that changes the way documents are written -- or rather, numbers are written to such a degree that it really cannot be done. Let me tell you another thing. I'm against what you would call en passant expertise because as my Professor Bishof said, it's like if you're reading somebody else's newspaper in the underground, over his shoulder. I hope you understand me to be saying this with the best of intentions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think I do understand, and that's the reason I'm asking you the question because it seems to me that even the best or maybe even especially the best handwriting expert would be reluctant to express that kind of opinion based on one number written in a small box and looking at another numeral 2 written in another small box to conclude that they were written by the same person, but that seems to be what you did in answering that question to Mr. Ackerman. Are you comfortable that that's a sufficient sample upon which to conclude that the same person wrote both numeral 2s, the one you saw in line number 29 and the one you see here in line 82?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that question. I have to tell you one thing. It is quite clear that this kind of list should not have any handwritten corrections. However, now that they're there, that they're anyway, I simply had to observe that it was done by two persons. If someone were to go to the archives and if you'd talk to these people, then they'd quickly tell you who did what because obviously one number 2 was made by Mr. Ademovski -- Mladenovski, whatever his name was, and the other 2 is someone else's. But I thought that it is important that the Court should know that two persons had intervened there, and of course what I'm telling you now about these boxes and how they're filled out, of course that has an effect too. For example, in case of the number 2, that can be a simple one, if it is entered in a box like that, then the termination is a bit abbreviated in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you what I understand the evidence from Mr. Mladenovski was regarding these handwritten changes in this document. As I recall his evidence, and I'm sure I'll be corrected if I state it inaccurately, but he claims that he made all the handwritten changes on this document except for the changes in line number 82. Now, if that's the case, it seems that he's saying he's the author of the handwritten numeral 2 that we looked at a little bit ago in line 29 and not the author of anything handwritten in line number 82. That seems to be inconsistent with what I understood you to say your opinion was that the handwritten numeral 2 in line 82 and in line 29 were by the same person. Do you have a comment about that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Of course. Thank you for that question. Please look at number 82. It has that romantic name, doesn't it, if we can put it that way. There's that swan. 84 is different already. I think that you don't have to be a rocket scientist to realize that these are two different persons. I don't know what Mr. Mladenovski said, but not both of those entries are his. One is, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But I understood him to say that the entry in line number 29 that we looked at was not his, even though upon viewing it, it does appear to have a bit of a swan's neck, to use your term. Now, is it still your opinion that the handwritten numeral 2 in item 29, line number 29, was written by the same person who wrote the handwritten numeral 2s in line 82 that's on the screen right now?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, I see 82, and that number 2 is not the same like the 2 in 84. I think that you will easily agree to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do agree to that. Could we go back for a minute, though, and look at the handwritten numeral 2 in line 29 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's see if we can get them side by side, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's a great idea, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Hannis, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that big enough, or should we try to enlarge it a little bit more?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: It's fine. Just tell me the number, please, 82 or 2 -- or rather, 84?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you look at first line number 29, that handwritten numeral 2.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then line number 82, the handwritten numeral 2s in that line.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness. Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, Professor, the interpreters cannot hear you. Could you start the answer again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. What was the other number after 782?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Line number 29 on the left.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [In English] 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want you to look at that numeral 2 and compare it to the numeral 2s in line number 82, and when you speak your answer, you may have to lean back from the screen a bit so the microphones will pick you up.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's do it in the right order. 29 that you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, compared to 82.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [In English] To 82. [Interpretation] I think -- of course it would be better if I had my instruments here if I were doing this properly, but I think this has to do with an abbreviated writing of the numeral 2 in the case of 29, 2. As for 82, the 2 is crossed out and it's too wide. I think that there is a certain difference, but I would have to do this properly in peace and magnify it 20 times, up to 40 times, so that I could see the end in 29. Yes, 29. Yes. It's hard to compare, but I think it can be done. But right now I cannot because number 2, the numeral 2, in number 29 is written in an abbreviated way. Yes. Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understood from your written report and supplement and what you said before that your review of the handwritten changes, numbers, in this document led you to conclude that there were two different writers of all of those handwritten changes. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is it your opinion that there were only two different writers, or could there have been more than two?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to tell you that this number 2, the one without any ornaments, the horizontal one, whereas this other 2 that has romantically been termed swan-like is only in a few other places. I haven't found others. Now, you can look at 3 and number 8, but I think it's only two persons that were involved in doing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You used another term when we were talking about the numerator and the stamp-pad. You talked about Gullivers. Can you tell me, is that a literary term from Gulliver's Travels?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Gulliver.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what are you referring to? You're referring to an exceptionally large number --

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [In English] Calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Large calibre.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [In English] Calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think just two more areas. In connection with -- I think it was the Exhibit -- I guess we were looking at the entry for number 248, and this is in Exhibit 3D 1131, item number 247 and 248. If we could have a look at that. Mr. Ackerman asked you to look at some digits that were written there and render an opinion about whether the same person wrote those. Can we enlarge the upper left quadrant as much as possible. Okay. Professor, you see that on the right-hand side of your screen at the very top, there is a handwritten 872-137/1, and about five lines below that in that column there's an 872-94/1-2. Do you recall looking at that earlier?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I do. Of course I do. I am grateful to you for going back to that question that I did not manage to answer because of the break. General similarity is established in terms of handwriting expertise, and it is eliminatory, and then there are individual characteristics that confirm who the scriptor was. In this case there is a general similarity; however, as for individual ones, I mean, I hope you won't hold it against me. I wouldn't dare do this without a proper instrument, but I would do that because the general similarity would compel me to do an expert report on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, that's what I wanted to clear up. Would you agree with me that's really a pretty small sample to try and reach a conclusion that those two entries were written by the same person?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the general similarity is there. As for individual similarity, that would require the peace and quiet of a lab and proper instruments so that I could tell you with a greater degree of certainty. As I told you, en passant expertise is not advisable in this profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And one possible reason for that similarity is because, indeed, they may have been done by the same person. That's one explanation, right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Another possible explanation is the second one, the 872-94, is written by someone who's trying to duplicate the handwriting in the earlier entry. That's possible too, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. If I may just analyse it this way. Now, although I said that this should be studied in particular. Please look at 248, this 872. Look at the 7. It is quite slanted, whereas the 7 up there is relatively vertical. However, I'm just referring to a finesse here that would have to be confirmed. Also, you should bear in mind that they're handwriting variants of the same script. No one writes the same way twice, but they do preserve their basic original characteristics.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree with you, Professor. Looking at my own signature, it varies from month to month, year to year. But I note in the 872-94 entry that I think you said before it appeared to be a different writing implement, but it appears that at least portions of that number appear to have been gone over more than once --

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: A bit slanted, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: The 7 is a bit slanted, don't you think? Down here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, but it looks to me as though perhaps part of the number 8 and part of the number 4 and perhaps part of the number 9 have been gone over more than once?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that is something that involves a new job.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And the last area I wanted to ask you about, I guess, was that -- I think you already answered. That's really too small a sample to try and reach an expert opinion on sitting here in the courtroom, right?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, one of the exhibits you put to the witness at the beginning of your evidence was 3D 1109, which is a log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, where does that feature in his reports or evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, 3D 1109 is the same document as 3D 1131.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've previously withdrawn 3D 1109 as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, because we had a problem with translation. At that point in time, the translation section didn't want to translate what was not clear. Later on, we received the translation, we uploaded it into the system, and it is there now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But if it's the same as 3D 1131, why do we have it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need it, Your Honours, because this page, 248 -- or rather, page 2 on which you can see both documents, so page 2 in both documents, this line in the first document, 1109, was not covered. We received the document without any restrictions whatsoever. We believe this to be important because it shows that in column 250, if you look at it, on that page in column 250 where the date is, 26th of May, no entry was made about the document, which means that it was a test of something similar. We will be drawing appropriate conclusions about that later on. So if you look at 1109 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But don't move just for the moment. Is this not a redacted version?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm getting no interpretation. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [In English] Oh, I'm sorry. [Interpretation] We have 1130 here, but if you look at 1109 -- [In English] 1130.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But 1130 is an archive list. 1109 is a log-book. Let's concentrate on the issue. My concern is with the log-book, 3D 1109.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [In English] I'm sorry, that's my mistake. [Interpretation] The log-book 1109 is the same document as 1130.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this the situation where --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 1131, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- one of them was redacted and the other one was simply a few -- page 1 and then a leap to page 7 or something like that of the same document?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that happened in both cases, both with the log-book and the archive list. We had the same situation there in both cases. In the first version, we received unredacted documents; and in the second version, we received redacted documents but complete ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why did you withdraw 3D 1109 and now try to introduce it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We withdrew 1109 because at that point we still did not have the translation from the CLSS because the copy was bad, illegible. Later on, they produced the translation, and it is attached to the document now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that document will be admitted through this witness. Do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a couple of brief questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, Mr. Ackerman questioned you. He put a number of questions to you about how could you work with colour photocopies, whether the colour depended on a printer, and whether it changed in various printing instances and so on. Would you now please look at the last page of 3D 1134, please. It will come up on the screen before you. This is the decision of the National Council and conclusion of the government cabinet, and on the last page one can see what it is that you actually received. Did you work on the basis of a CD which also had a scanned colour document?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, scanned in the proper sense of the word, not doctored. So these were authentic copies, quite appropriate for expertise, but had I not seen them in the original, I would not have been as firm as I was about saying that the document had not been abused.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: All right. So the government did not provide to us a colour photocopy but, rather, a document that was scanned?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, scanned, but different type of scanning. Today, when one uses that term, scanning, that means transferring somebody's signature from one document to another. In the case that you're describing, scanning refers to a very good quality of copying.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see the last page of both documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're -- are we not on the last page?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I just wanted to draw your attention to the last page of the document where you can see what it is that the cabinet -- government cabinet of Serbia provided to the Ojdanic Defence and we later in turn to Professor Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Professor, my next question deals with document IC -- I apologise, IC 196. I will kindly ask that it be put on the ELMO -- rather, a different copy be placed on the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on, please, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Professor, you talked to me about similarities and differences of numerators. You showed it in a copy containing seven rather than eight of dates. Now, this eighth column that can be seen on the picture before you, does it change anything in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, the one on the screen only has seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on the ELMO we have the one with eight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, the last record of a reference here to an exhibit is to document IC 196. Now, that is if you press your e-court button on the screen. What is it you're now showing the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I'm showing to him another document that contains a total of eight imprints rather than IC 196, which has seven dates.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I reply?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it a coloured copy? Is it black and white? What is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a coloured copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. So that's now on the ELMO, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may answer. The most important ones for analysis are the first two imprints. The remaining ones, regardless of whether there were a total of seven or eight, they only serve the purpose of showing the difference in the calibre in the first two. So that's the only difference. The first two are absolute, and the remaining ones show what a typical, a regular, imprint looked like, whether it was the seventh or the eighth, it's -- it makes no difference from number 2 down. Everything is typical.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you directly. What you see on the ELMO in front of you --

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: -- and what you testified about today concerning Exhibit 1C 196, you actually make no difference or no changes when it comes to the substance of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. As I've told you, everything below the second imprint is there just to serve as an illustration.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Professor, today you testified and said that you heard the testimony of Witness Mladenovski, that you followed it. Can you tell me, what did you hear?

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard it when I arrived here, and then I checked some internet sites, and I found some information. But to tell you the truth, as soon as I saw that Mladenovski admitted to everything, as I've told you, I was quite satisfied. And if I may say so, I expected to have an easier time testifying here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We still have this remaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we be given the IC number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC 198, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I have just a question for him. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, learned Professor, it's a question more to deal in the territory of academics. I've always been of the -- I've been thinking that this science of handwriting expertise, of finding out handwriting or identifying handwriting is not a perfect science as compared to the finger-prints, and that is why we find that on documents you require witnesses to say that this is the handwriting of such and such person. Do you agree with that statement, or would you like to enlighten me on this subject? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: ZIVOJIN ALEKSIC
utterances.text: First of all, we have the following terms: Graphology, graphoscopy, graphometrics, and all of that speaks of how that field developed. As the new implements or means were brought in, it became an uncertain -- or rather, it used to be an uncertain discipline that caused numerous problems in French legislation, and then it became sort of more sure of itself, if I may say so. And what is difficult in this field is that it is impossible to establish the date of handwriting [as interpreted] and that it is possible to give several interpretations. So from that point of view, you are right. It is not an exact science, but many things can be established by handwriting expertise. For example, if people are not satisfied with last wills, they ask for a psychiatric evaluation without going into handwriting or signature evaluation. However, there are sufficient elements to believe that handwriting expertise will maintain its place in the evidentiary proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 85 -- or rather, page 85, line 7, Professor said age of ink -- or rather, date of ink, and it says here the date of handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming here to assist us. You may now leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President and members of the Trial Chamber, thank you for allowing me to sit while I testified. Please accept my apologies if I created any difficulty for you rather than assisting you through my testimony. I devoted my entire life to expertise, and I was an expert in many courts, and Aristotle used to say when you go to court, you go to get justice. I hope that I was true to that role on this occasion as well. Thank you to the Prosecutor and to the Defence. Good-bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, I don't think anyone would disagree with me when I say that we found your evidence very interesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But, Professor, I have a suggestion. Would you like to suggest Mr. Ackerman as a student in the future?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] No. I think Mr. Ackerman and me, we are really different. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And you don't want to indoctrinate him --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] You know, but I must tell you something, because sometimes coming in a situation to the accused, I take advocate Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The Professor's influence is probably even greater than he thinks himself because for him, time has stood still, and the clock will now allow us to have another two witnesses, I think, tonight. It is, in fact, after ten minutes to 7.00, so there is little point in trying to commence the evidence of another witness tonight. So we shall now adjourn -- sorry, Mr. Visnjic wants us to stay. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, just briefly. In the meantime while I was questioning Professor Aleksic, your decision arrived, your ruling, on the motion to withdraw the expert on behalf of General Pavkovic's Defence, and for the record I'd like to say two things, the first one being that we haven't received the correspondence, which must be a technical error, and that's why we were unable to respond to it; and the second one is that on the following day after Witness Mladenovski testified, so on the following day, his mobile number was delivered to the Defence of General Pavkovic, and he received a call for the first time on the 5th of May to provide samples, which is what he did right away. So I'd like to say that in no way did we affect or influence any conclusions relating to that because I see that that is listed down as one of the reasons for withdrawing this expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, once you've had time to digest the decision, I'm sure you will discover that it deals with all the situations that you might have been concerned about, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There was absolutely no claim in that regard, Your Honour. It was holiday season in Belgrade, and you couldn't find anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We shall adjourn now until tomorrow at 9.00 in Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
